What Does “Heaven and Earth” Mean in the Bible? The Answer Changes Everything

September 6, 2026
By Levaire

Share

Facebook
X
Pinterest
WhatsApp
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by

    Instaread

    Most readers come to the Bible with a picture already in place. Heaven is up there, clouds, light, angels, the throne of God. Earth is down here, soil, nations, history, us. When the Bible says “heaven and earth,” we hear cosmos. We hear universe. We hear everything that exists.

    That picture is not wrong exactly. But it is incomplete in ways that distort some of the most important passages in Scripture. Because the Bible uses “heaven and earth” to mean something else entirely: something its original readers would have recognized immediately, something that has been largely lost in the translation from ancient Jewish thought to modern Western Christianity.

    Once you see it, you cannot unsee it. And once you cannot unsee it, whole portions of Isaiah, Jeremiah, the Gospels, 2 Peter, and Revelation begin to mean something quite different than what you were told they meant.

    This article is an attempt to show you what the biblical writers meant when they spoke of heaven and earth, and why that meaning matters more than most Christians have been taught to think.

    How Many Heavens Does the Bible Describe?

    Before we can understand what “heaven and earth” means symbolically, we need to establish what it means literally, because the Bible uses the word “heaven” in at least three distinct ways and conflating them is the first source of confusion.

    The first heaven is the sky: the atmospheric heavens, the domain of weather, birds, and clouds. Isaiah 55:10 uses this heaven when it describes rain and snow coming down from heaven to water the earth. This is simply the sky.

    The second heaven is the celestial realm: the stars, planets, and the vast expanse of the cosmos. Psalm 19:1-6 uses this heaven: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands.” This is the astronomical universe.

    The third heaven is the dwelling place of God: what Paul refers to in 2 Corinthians 12:2 when he describes being “caught up to the third heaven.” This is the divine realm, the place where God’s throne is, inaccessible to human beings under ordinary circumstances.

    Modern readers tend to flatten these three into one and assume every biblical reference to “heaven” means the third: the realm of God. This creates immediate problems, because the biblical writers moved freely between all three and sometimes used “heaven” to mean none of them.

    When “Heaven and Earth” Means Rulers and Nations

    Here is the idea that unlocks the passage most readers miss: in the prophetic literature of the Hebrew Bible, “heaven and earth” frequently refers not to the cosmos but to a ruling class and the nation it governs. The rulers and authorities, kings, priests, the governing order, are the heaven. The people under them are the earth.

    This is not a modern interpretive invention. It is rooted in the ancient Near Eastern understanding of the cosmos as a reflection of the political and social order, and it surfaces explicitly across the ANE world and then directly inside the biblical text when you know to look for it.

    Across the ancient Near East, the structure of heaven mirrored the structure of earthly governance. The gods of Mesopotamia ruled the cosmos the way kings ruled their kingdoms: in councils, with hierarchies, with designated territories and responsibilities. The heavenly realm was not a separate reality disconnected from human affairs. It was the divine template from which human political order derived its legitimacy. Kings ruled because the gods had authorized them. Nations existed because divine powers governed them. The cosmic and the political were two sides of the same reality.

    This framework appears inside the Hebrew Bible most strikingly in Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32. Psalm 82 opens with God presiding over an assembly of elohim, divine beings whom he charges with corrupt governance: “How long will you defend the unjust and show partiality to the wicked?” (v.2). These beings have been assigned authority over the nations, and God is calling them to account for how they have exercised it. The psalm ends with God reclaiming jurisdiction: “Rise up, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are your inheritance” (v.8). The heavenly assembly, the ruling powers above the nations, is the direct ANE backdrop for Israel’s understanding of how the cosmos operated.

    Deuteronomy 32:8-9 makes this even more explicit. In the oldest reading of the text, preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls, God divided the nations at Babel “according to the number of the sons of God,” assigning each nation to a divine being while retaining Israel as his own inheritance. The nations had heavenly counterparts, heavenly rulers. The heaven above each nation was, in the most concrete sense, the divine power governing it.

    Isaiah 14 offers a further illustration. The famous passage about the “morning star, son of the dawn” falling from heaven (v.12) is almost universally applied in popular Christianity to Satan’s original fall. But read in context, it is explicitly addressed to the king of Babylon (v.4): “You will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon.” The falling of the heavenly figure is the political and spiritual destruction of the Babylonian ruling order. The language is cosmic because the ruler was understood to be a cosmic entity as well as a political one, the earthly king reflecting the heavenly prince behind him. Heaven falls when its earthly representative falls.

    Isaiah 1 opens with what sounds like a cosmic address: “Hear, O heavens! Listen, O earth! For the LORD has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2). But read the next few verses and it becomes clear that God is not addressing the cosmos. He is addressing Israel: specifically its corrupt leaders and people. Verse 10 makes it explicit: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom; listen to the instruction of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” The heavens are the rulers. The earth is the people. The cosmos is not in view at all.

    Jeremiah 22:29 uses the same construction: “O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!” This is addressed to the nation of Judah under the shadow of Babylonian judgment: not to the literal ground beneath their feet, but to the people and their governing order.

    Isaiah 34: Stars Falling, Sky Rolling Up — Edom’s Day of the Lord

    The clearest and most dramatic illustration of this principle is Isaiah 34. Read verses 3 and 4 in isolation and you will almost certainly conclude you are reading about the end of the universe:

    “Their slain will be left unburied, and the stench of their corpses will rise; the mountains will be soaked with their blood. All the stars of the heavens will be dissolved and the sky rolled up like a scroll; all the starry host will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like shriveled figs from the fig tree.”

    Stars dissolving. The sky rolled up like a scroll. Every starry host falling. This sounds like Judgment Day: the literal, cosmic, final end of all things. This is exactly the kind of language that fuels prophecy conferences and end-times speculation.

    But keep reading. Verses 5 and 6 identify the subject:

    “My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; see, it descends in judgment on Edom and on the people I have totally destroyed. The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood, it is covered with fat: the blood of lambs and goats, fat from the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.”

    Edom. A specific nation with a specific capital city, Bozrah. The dissolving of the heavens and the rolling up of the sky is the language Isaiah uses to describe the political and military destruction of the Edomite ruling order. The stars that fall are not celestial bodies: they are the rulers and authorities of Edom, falling like leaves from a vine.

    And lest anyone argue that Edom is being used as a symbol for something larger and still-future, notice that verses 3 and 10 include rotting bodies and “ensuing generations”: the ordinary aftermath of historical military conquest, not the end of all things.

    The sky is not falling. The ruling order of Edom is falling. The language is apocalyptic. The event is historical.

    And the event did happen. Edom’s Day of the Lord came at the hands of Babylon. The Babylonian campaigns of the late seventh and early sixth centuries BC brought devastation to the surrounding nations, and Edom, which had opportunistically aided Babylon in the sack of Jerusalem in 587 BC, found itself subject to the same imperial judgment it had helped unleash on others. This is the conquering in view when Isaiah’s cosmic language ignites: not the extinction of every Edomite, but the destruction of Edom as a sovereign nation, its ruling order shattered by a foreign army directed by God himself. The stars that fell were Edom’s kings and princes. The heavens that dissolved were their authority.

    What followed was a long decline, worth noting but distinct from the Day of the Lord itself. Edom never recovered as a political entity. The Babylonian king Nabonidus further devastated the region around 553 BC. The Nabataean Arabs pressed in from the south and east over the following centuries, eventually making Petra their capital on what had been Edomite soil. The Edomites who survived migrated west into Idumea. It was from this remnant that Herod the Great descended. By 70 AD, the Idumeans were destroyed alongside Jerusalem in Rome’s obliteration of the Jewish revolt, ending the last traceable remnant of the Edomite people. The land today is desolate terrain in southern Jordan.

    But notice what this pattern establishes. Isaiah’s cosmic de-creation language, the stars dissolving, the sky rolled up, the host of heaven falling, describes the conquest and collapse of a ruling order. It is the precise mirror image of the new heaven and new earth creation language the prophets use when a new covenant order is being established. De-creation and new creation are the same vocabulary deployed from opposite directions, describing the same kind of event: the end of one ruling heaven-and-earth and the beginning of another. When you understand that the Day of the Lord language is always cosmic de-creation pointing to a historical conquest, and that new creation language is always cosmic re-creation pointing to a new covenant order, the whole prophetic imagination snaps into focus. The prophets are not describing the physics of the universe. They are describing the theology of history.

    The Temple as Heaven and Earth: Where God and Israel Met

    To understand the full weight of the heaven-and-earth framework, you need to understand what the Temple meant to ancient Israel, because the Temple was not merely a religious building. It was understood to be the literal point where heaven met earth.

    The first-century Jewish historian Josephus explains this in his Antiquities of the Jews (3.7.7), where he describes how Moses designed the tabernacle, the portable predecessor to the Temple, in three sections. The outer court represented the land and sea and was therefore accessible to all. The inner court represented heaven. The innermost sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, was the dwelling place of God: inaccessible to all except the High Priest, once a year, because heaven itself is inaccessible to human beings.

    The symbolism ran throughout the entire structure. The twelve loaves of showbread represented the twelve months of the year. The seven-branched candlestick represented the seven known planets. The four-part veil represented the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Even the High Priest’s vestments represented creation itself. The Temple was a miniature cosmos, and standing in it was standing at the intersection of the divine and the human.

    Psalm 78:69 captures this: God “built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth he established forever.” The sanctuary is heaven-and-earth. It is the place where those two realities converge.

    This is why, when the prophets speak of judgment against Israel and its Temple, they reach for cosmic language. The Temple was the cosmos, symbolically speaking. Its destruction was, from within the world of ancient Jewish thought, the end of the world: not the physical world, but the world-as-ordered-by-God’s-covenant-with-Israel. The heaven-and-earth of the Mosaic system.

    Why Israel Was Called Heaven and Earth

    The Temple’s symbolic identity extended to the nation that housed it. Because Israel was the people raised up to be God’s own possession, separated from the nations as the dry land was separated from the sea in Genesis 1:9-10, and because Israel hosted the Temple, and therefore God himself, the nation of Israel extended the heaven-and-earth imagery to herself.

    Israel was the heaven-and-earth of the Old Covenant. Its rulers were its heaven. Its people were its earth. And its covenant relationship with God gave it a cosmic significance that no other nation possessed.

    This is why prophetic language about judgment against Israel consistently sounds like the end of everything. When the prophets speak of God shaking the heavens and moving the earth, they are often describing the destabilization of the Israelite covenant order: the removal of kings, the fall of the priesthood, the devastation of the land. To those inside the system, it felt like the universe was ending. The prophets used language that matched that feeling while describing events that were historical and specific.

    Revelation 12 gives us one of the most vivid illustrations of this Israel-as-heaven-and-earth identity. The chapter opens with a stunning vision: “A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (v.1). Read in isolation, this sounds like pure cosmic spectacle. But the imagery is not original to John. It comes directly from Joseph’s dream in Genesis 37:9-10, where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow down to him. Jacob interprets the dream without hesitation: the sun is Jacob himself, the moon is his wife, the stars are his sons — the twelve patriarchs of Israel. John’s first-century Jewish readers would have recognized the source material immediately.

    The woman of Revelation 12, then, is not a literal cosmic figure. She is clothed in the heaven-and-earth imagery of Israel — the sun and moon of its patriarchal order, the twelve stars of its twelve tribes. She is the covenant people, faithful Israel, from whom the Messiah came. The child she bears is identified explicitly as “one who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter” (v.5), the language of Psalm 2 applied to the Messiah. The dragon waiting to devour the child is the spiritual power behind Rome, the same beast of Daniel 7 driving the empire that crucified Jesus and persecuted his followers.

    What Revelation 12 shows us is the heaven-and-earth framework working from the inside out. Israel’s cosmic identity, her standing as the heaven-and-earth of the covenant, is written into the very image of the woman. And when the child is caught up to God and his throne (v.5) and the woman flees into the wilderness to a place prepared for her (v.6), we are watching the transition the whole article has been building toward. The faithful remnant of Israel, now expanded to include Gentile believers, becomes the Church — the new covenant community — without ceasing to be the same woman, the same people, the same covenant story. She does not become something else. She becomes what she was always meant to be. The heaven-and-earth of the old covenant gives way to the heaven-and-earth of the new, and the people of God carry the identity through the transition.

    What Does Isaiah 65 Say About the New Heaven and New Earth?

    With this framework in place, Isaiah 65 opens up in ways that would otherwise remain closed.

    Isaiah 65:17 announces: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.”

    Most readers hear this and think: physical universe, end times, the eternal state. But Isaiah does not let that reading stand for long. By verse 20, he is describing infant mortality, sinners being cursed at a hundred years old, people building houses and planting vineyards. These are the conditions of ordinary human life: not the eternal state, where there is no death, no sin, and no aging.

    The new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65 are not a physical re-creation of the cosmos. They are the New Covenant order, the ruling reality inaugurated by the Messiah, in which the old heaven-and-earth of the Mosaic system has been replaced by something new. A new covenant. A new priesthood. A new way of relating to God, not through the Temple and its sacrifices but through the body and blood of the one the Temple always pointed toward.

    The parallels between Isaiah 65 and Revelation 21 are not coincidental: they are identical in structure. In both passages, God creates the new heavens and new earth. In both, the former things are not remembered. In both, mourning and weeping cease. In both, a holy city is present. In both, God’s people receive a new identity. John in Revelation is deliberately quoting Isaiah 65, which means the new heaven and new earth of Revelation 21 is the same new heaven and new earth of Isaiah 65: the New Covenant kingdom of God, not a literal cosmic re-creation.

    Paul understood this. In 2 Corinthians 5:17, he writes: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” Paul is not describing what will happen at the end of history. He is describing what has already happened in the person who has come into covenant relationship with God through Christ. The new creation is present tense. The old has passed away. The new has come.

    What Does 2 Peter 3 Really Describe? Heaven, Earth, and 70 AD

    The dissolution language of 2 Peter 3 has been perhaps the most misread passage in the entire heaven-and-earth conversation. Peter describes the heavens passing away “with a great noise,” the elements melting “with fervent heat,” and the earth and its works being “burned up” (v.10).

    For centuries, readers have taken this as a description of the literal, physical destruction of the universe at the end of history. But this reading runs directly into the same problem as Isaiah 34: the Day of the Lord, which Peter places this event within, is consistently a term used in the Old Testament not for the end of the cosmos but for God’s judgment against a specific nation at the hands of an invading army.

    Amos, Joel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel: all use “Day of the Lord” language to describe historical, national judgments: against Babylon, against Egypt, against Edom, against Israel itself. The cosmic imagery is the idiom. The events are historical.

    And for 2 Peter 3, the first-century Jewish historian Josephus provides a remarkable witness. In his account of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in 70 AD, he describes the event in language that matches Peter’s almost exactly:

    “The flame was also carried a long way, and made an echo, together with the groans of those that were slain… one would have thought the whole city had been on fire. Nor can one imagine any thing either greater, or more terrible than this noise.” (Wars 6.5.1)

    To a first-century Jew, the Temple was the place where heaven met earth. Watching it dissolve in fire, the screaming, the blood, the collapse of the entire Mosaic order, was not merely the destruction of a building. It was the end of the world. The old heaven and earth, the covenant order of Moses, was passing away exactly as Peter and Jesus had said it would.

    Jesus himself, predicting Jerusalem’s fall from the Mount of Olives, said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away” (Matthew 24:35, Mark 13:31, Luke 21:33). The heaven and earth he predicted would pass away did. His words did not.

    Revelation 21-22: New Heaven and New Earth or New Covenant?

    If the old heaven and earth was the Mosaic covenant order centered on the Temple, then the new heaven and new earth of Revelation 21 is the New Covenant order centered on Christ. This is not a reduction of the vision: it is the vision at its fullest and most immediate.

    But this reading has to contend with some of the most absolute language in the New Testament. “No more death or mourning or crying or pain” (21:4). “He who was seated on the throne said, ‘I am making everything new'” (21:5). “No longer will there be any curse” (22:3). How can these statements describe the New Covenant when Christians still die, still mourn, still experience pain?

    The question assumes that these promises refer to the physical conditions of the believer’s earthly life. But look carefully at what has changed and what has not.

    What has changed is the covenantal reality. Under the Old Covenant, infant death was a curse: a literal, explicit sign of God’s judgment against a nation that had broken his law (Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28). Physical suffering was covenant punishment. The death of a child was theological condemnation written in human loss. Under the New Covenant, Christ has borne the entire curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). Physical death and suffering still occur, but they are no longer signs of divine condemnation. They are the ordinary conditions of a fallen world that still groans toward its final redemption (Romans 8:22). The curse of the law, the covenant curse, has been removed entirely.

    The “no more death” of Revelation 21:4, read against John 11:25-26 — “Whoever believes in me will live, even though he dies; and whoever lives and believes in me will never die”: is a statement about covenantal and spiritual reality, not yet about physical conditions. The believer has crossed from death to life. The sting of death has been removed. Its power over the people of God has been broken. Those who are in Christ enter immediately into his presence upon physical death, no longer descending to Sheol to await redemption, for redemption has come.

    And then notice what Revelation 22:14-15 says, just one chapter after the establishment of the new heaven and new earth: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have the right to the tree of life and may go through the gates into the city. Outside are the dogs, those who practice magic arts, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.”

    Outside. Sinners, still sinning, still outside the city. If the new heaven and new earth of Revelation 21 described the eternal, physical, post-judgment state, there would be no one left outside: all the unrighteous would already be in the lake of fire (Revelation 20:15). The city with its open gates and its nations coming and going and its sinners still on the outside is not the eternal state. It is the New Covenant kingdom, living and active in the present age, with gates wide open to all who will enter and an outside that remains for those who will not.

    How to Read Biblical “Heaven and Earth” Language Correctly

    The ancient Jewish understanding of heaven and earth was not merely a poetic convention. It was a theological framework that shaped how the prophets communicated, how Jesus taught, how the apostles wrote, and how the earliest Christians read their Scriptures.

    When that framework is lost, as it largely has been in Western Christianity, readers are left trying to make literal sense of language that was never intended to be literal, and symbolic sense of language that was intended to be taken with full seriousness. The result is a Christianity that perpetually relocates its most important promises to a distant future, unable to inhabit what has already been given.

    The new heavens and the new earth are not coming. They have come: inaugurated in the life, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ, and in the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost. The old covenant order, the old heaven and earth of the Mosaic system, has passed away. The new is here.

    This does not mean history is over, or that physical creation does not await its own redemption (Romans 8:19-21). It means that the covenant reality, the ruling order, the heaven-and-earth in its biblical sense, has already been transformed. The kingdom of God is not coming. It is here, advancing, filling the earth the way leaven fills dough, the way a mustard seed becomes a tree.

    The question is not whether you are waiting for the new heaven and new earth. The question is whether you know you are already living in it.

    Key References and Further Reading

    Beale, G.K. The Temple and the Church’s Mission: A Biblical Theology of the Dwelling Place of God. InterVarsity Press, 2004. The standard scholarly treatment of the Temple as a cosmic symbol in its ANE context, and of Revelation 21-22 as eschatological temple. Publisher page: ivpress.com. Amazon: amazon.com/dp/0830826181

    Gentry, Kenneth. Before Jerusalem Fell: Dating the Book of Revelation. American Vision, 1998. For the preterist framework underlying the reading of Revelation in this article.

    Heiser, Michael S. The Unseen Realm: Recovering the Supernatural Worldview of the Bible. Lexham Press, 2015. The primary accessible treatment of the divine council, Psalm 82, and the ANE background to Deuteronomy 32:8-9. Publisher page: lexhampress.com. Heiser’s academic paper on Deuteronomy 32:8 specifically: thedivinecouncil.com

    Josephus, Flavius. Antiquities of the Jews 3.7.7 (on the tabernacle’s cosmic symbolism). Full text: penelope.uchicago.edu

    Josephus, Flavius. Wars of the Jews 6.5.1 (on the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD). Full text: penelope.uchicago.edu

    Schoenherr, Matthew. Prophetic Imagery (on heaven and earth). Prophecy Course. Full text: prophecycourse.org

    Wright, N.T. The New Testament and the People of God. Fortress Press, 1992. For the Jewish cosmic symbolism framework and the heaven-and-earth imagery of the covenant.

    On the Deuteronomy 32:8 textual question (“sons of Israel” vs. “sons of God”), see the Biblical Archaeology Society’s overview: library.biblicalarchaeology.org
